title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Umbilical arterial catheterization involves placement of a catheter into one of the neonatal umbilical arteries to obtain reliable arterial access during critical illness. The umbilical artery constricts shortly after birth but remains cannulable for several days, enabling continuous blood pressure monitoring, frequent arterial blood sampling, and the administration of fluids or medications. Proper positioning requires radiographic confirmation, and ongoing vigilance reduces the risk of thrombosis, vascular spasm, hemorrhage, infection, or organ ischemia. This procedure offers substantial clinical value but carries potentially serious complications, making precise technique and careful monitoring essential for safe use in extremely premature or unstable neonates.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Continuing Education Activity
content: The learning activity guides participants through relevant anatomy, depth estimation, procedural steps, troubleshooting strategies, and evidence-based management principles for umbilical arterial catheterization. Instruction emphasizes structured communication and shared decision-making among clinicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, and radiology personnel, allowing the interprofessional team to coordinate placement, confirm catheter position, and monitor for early signs of complications. Collaborative practice enhances accuracy, promotes timely intervention, and supports safer care delivery, ultimately improving neonatal outcomes and reducing procedure-related morbidity.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Introduction
content: Umbilical arterial catheterization offers direct access to the arterial system, enabling arterial blood sampling and continuous systemic blood pressure monitoring. The procedure is commonly performed in extremely premature neonates and, while technically straightforward, requires consistent practice for proficiency. [1] Complications such as infection, thrombosis, or vascular injury may occur when placement or maintenance is suboptimal.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The umbilical artery originates from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. In fetal life, the artery traverses the umbilical cord, carrying deoxygenated blood from the fetus back to the placenta (see Image. Infant With Umbilical Catheter). Usually, there are 2 umbilical arteries and 1 umbilical vein within the umbilical cord. The 2 umbilical arteries have smaller, thick-walled lumens and are typically inferior to the umbilical vein, which has a larger, thin-walled lumen. The prenatal identification of an isolated single umbilical artery appears to be associated with a higher risk of small-for-gestational-age neonates and preterm delivery. [2]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: There are 2 potential positions for umbilical artery catheterization. The "high position" is at the level of T6–T9 above the diaphragm and above the celiac artery (T12), superior mesenteric artery (T12–L1), and renal arteries (L1). The "low position" is at L3–L4 just above the aortic bifurcation (L4–L5). The catheter tip placed in the descending aorta at the high position is associated with lower risks of vascular insufficiency, thrombus formation, and extremity cyanosis; this is usually the preferred position for umbilical artery catheterization. The optimal catheter placement can be calculated using body-measurement-based or anatomic-landmark-based formulas discussed below. [3] [4]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Indications
content: The primary indications for umbilical artery catheterization include frequent arterial blood gas measurements, blood sampling, or continuous blood pressure monitoring in extremely low-birthweight infants or critically ill neonates. Occasionally, it can be used temporarily to infuse parenteral nutrition when alternate access is unavailable. [5] An umbilical arterial catheter can be lifesaving in managing critically ill neonates.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Indications
content: However, the risks and benefits must be carefully weighed before attempting the procedure, as it carries potential complications. Very low birth weight infants (with less than 1000 g body weight), preterm infants who need mechanical ventilator support, infants with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy undergoing therapeutic hypothermia, and critically ill late preterm or term infants requiring mechanical ventilation are some of the groups of neonates who benefit from the use of an umbilical arterial catheter due to the need for frequent blood sampling. [3]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Contraindications
content: Contraindications to umbilical arterial catheterization include omphalitis, necrotizing enterocolitis, omphalocele, gastroschisis, and peritonitis. [6] These conditions increase the risk of infection, impaired perfusion, or worsening abdominal pathology. Clinicians should avoid catheter placement in these scenarios to prevent additional complications and ensure neonatal safety.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Preparation
content: Proper preparation is essential to ensure safe and effective umbilical artery catheterization. Key steps, including determining the appropriate catheter depth, help minimize complications and optimize placement in critically ill neonates.
contents: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Preparation. Proper preparation is essential to ensure safe and effective umbilical artery catheterization. Key steps, including determining the appropriate catheter depth, help minimize complications and optimize placement in critically ill neonates.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Preparation -- Depth of Catheterization
content: After determining the need for an umbilical arterial catheter, informed consent must be obtained in accordance with the local institutional policy. The ideal position of the catheter tip should be at the "high position" in the descending aorta, above the origins of the celiac, mesenteric, and renal arteries, to avoid occluding these vessels. This high position, in which the catheter tip lies above the diaphragm between T6 and T9, is preferred over the low position at L3 and L4 because it is associated with fewer complications and a reduced risk of thrombosis. [8] Several methods are used to determine the depth of insertion of the umbilical artery catheter. The Shukla and Wright formulas take into account the neonate's weight. The Shukla formula is as follows: Umbilical Artery Catheter Depth (cm) = (birth weight in kg x 3) + 9 [9] The Wright formula is as follows: Umbilical Artery Catheter Depth (cm) = (birth weight kg x 4) + 7 [9]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Preparation -- Depth of Catheterization
content: Gupta described an approach relying on anatomical landmarks to determine the depth of insertion rather than body weight. This approach relies on the distances from the umbilicus to nipple (UN) and from the umbilicus to the symphysis pubis (USp). This was thought to provide more accurate estimates of insertion length than body-weight-based formulas. The Gupta formula is as follows: Umbilical Artery Catheter Depth (cm) = (UN - 1 cm) + 2 USp [10] Other methods for estimating the depth of insertion are also described. [11] [12]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment
content: Successful umbilical artery catheterization requires a systematic, precise technique to ensure accurate placement and minimize complications. Clinicians must follow evidence-based procedural steps, maintain aseptic conditions, and carefully handle the catheter to protect the fragile vasculature of critically ill neonates. Attention to detail throughout the procedure is essential for optimal outcomes.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Catheter Placement
content: Before starting the procedure, the neonate must be restrained with soft arm and leg restraints to minimize movement. The neonate can be placed supine on a radiant warmer, with the head positioned at the top of the warmer to avoid hypothermia during the procedure. The umbilical cord and the surrounding skin are cleaned with an antiseptic solution. The catheter is prepared in a sterile fashion by connecting a 3-way stopcock to the catheter, connecting a 5-mL syringe to each port of the stopcock, and flushing the system with heparinized solution (0.45% sodium chloride plus 1:1 heparin) to ensure no air bubbles are present. The stopcock is then turned off to the catheter. The assistant holds up the umbilical cord with the cord clamp so that the physician/advanced practice provider can clean the cord and the skin 3 to 5 cm around the cord base with 4% chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine solution.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Catheter Placement
content: The abdomen is then draped, and an umbilical tie is placed around the cord. (Tie a square knot tight enough to minimize blood loss but loose enough to allow catheters to be passed easily through the vessels.) The cord is then cut horizontally with an 11-blade scalpel, 1 to 1.5 cm from the skin. The cord stump is grasped, and traction is applied.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Catheter Placement
content: Identify the vessels of the cord: 2 small muscular arteries with a thick lumen and 1 thin-walled umbilical vein. The lumen of 1 of the arteries is probed and gently dilated with the curved iris forceps. The tips of the iris forceps are used to spread open and dilate the lumen for 15 to 30 seconds. Once the artery is dilated, the catheter is then grasped approximately 1 cm from the tip with the curved iris forceps, or between the thumb and forefinger, and inserted into the lumen of the dilated artery.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Catheter Placement
content: Advance the catheter into the lumen to 2 cm deep, then remove the iris forceps. Continue advancing the catheter to 4 to 5 cm and aspirate to verify the lumen position. If blood is aspirated, the catheter is within the lumen. Clear the catheter by injecting 0.5 mL of heparinized solution.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Catheter Placement
content: Repeated probing or excessive pressure can result in vessel perforation. If unsuccessful, catheterization of the other artery must be attempted. Once the catheter is in place, an abdominal x-ray is performed to confirm proper positioning between the T6 and T9 vertebrae. On imaging, the catheter should be visualized entering the umbilical cord, diving inferiorly to connect with the internal iliac artery, then curving cephalad to enter the aorta between T6 and T9. The catheter can be retracted if needed, but it should never be advanced once it is secured due to the risk of introducing infection. However, the use of ultrasound guidance for umbilical catheter tip placement has become increasingly prevalent due to its demonstrated accuracy, cost-effectiveness, and enhanced safety profile. [13]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Catheter Placement
content: Once the position is confirmed, the catheter is secured using purse-string sutures around the base of the cord, and the tie is removed. Infusion of a heparinized solution must be started as soon as the catheter tip is verified to be in an appropriate position. Connect the arterial pressure transducer to verify the presence of proper arterial waveforms. [14]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Catheter Removal
content: Once the catheter is ready to be removed, stop any infusions, cut the suture around the base of the cord, and pull the catheter back by 1 cm to 2 cm. Wait approximately 5 to 10 minutes to allow for constriction of the umbilical artery. Once bleeding has stopped, remove the rest of the catheter. Place the neonate in the supine position for 30 to 60 minutes after removal to monitor for any bleeding. If bleeding occurs during catheter removal, apply pressure with umbilical tape around the base of the cord. [14]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Technique or Treatment -- Catheter Troubleshooting
content: Take the time to dilate the vessel, as this increases the likelihood of success and reduces the risk of perforating it or creating a false track. If there is any resistance to advancing the catheter, gentle, steady pressure must be applied. If there is a "popping" sensation during catheter advancement, it may indicate that the catheter has exited the lumen and created a false track. If this occurs, remove the catheter and use the second vessel for catheterization. If vessel spasm happens during insertion, use 0.5 mL of 2% lidocaine without epinephrine as a vasodilator, injecting it into the vessel while applying constant pressure until the artery is appropriately dilated. Do not advance the catheter once it is securely placed in the appropriate location, as this can significantly increase the risk of infection by introducing contaminated portions of the catheter. [15]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Complications
content: Thromboembolism is a major concern with the use of umbilical arterial catheters. Occlusion of the mesenteric arteries can result in gut ischemia, bowel infarction, and necrotizing enterocolitis. Renal artery involvement can lead to hypertension or acute renal failure. More distal vascular accidents can result in an ischemic injury to the back, buttocks, and lower extremities. Remove the catheter if there is any sign of vascular compromise. Other complications, such as vessel perforation, peritoneal perforation, bladder injury, and false aneurysm, can occur during catheter insertion.

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Complications
content: Catheter-associated infection and bleeding are other frequently associated complications. Umbilical artery catheters should be kept in place for no more than 5 days due to the risk of infection. Refractory hypoglycemia is a rare complication associated with high-position umbilical artery catheters whose tip is near the celiac and mesenteric arteries. [16] [17] [18] [19] There is a theoretical concern about the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants receiving enteral feedings while an umbilical arterial catheter is in place. However, there is no evidence supporting this, and withholding enteral feeds while an infant has an umbilical arterial catheter is no longer recommended.

content: An umbilical arterial catheter can be lifesaving in caring for critically ill neonates. However, the risks and benefits must be carefully weighed before attempting the procedure, as it carries potential complications. Adhering to guidelines that standardize the use of umbilical catheters in neonates is imperative. [22]

title: Umbilical Artery Catheterization -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: An interprofessional healthcare team approach is essential for the successful insertion and maintenance of umbilical arterial catheterization. This team will include advanced clinicians, specialists, mid-level practitioners, nursing staff, and surgical assistants, all with specialized neonatal care training. Communication and coordination between the clinicians/advanced practitioners and nurses are very important. The necessity of the catheter must be evaluated daily by the healthcare team, with nursing staff reporting any findings observed during care. The catheter must be removed when no longer necessary. [23] Continuation of the umbilical arterial catheter beyond 5 days is not recommended due to the risk of infection and thrombosis associated with its prolonged use. [24] [25]
